canberra.title: AI marketing is flooding our social feeds, but is it all slop in need of boycotting?
canberra.snippet: A new Instagram page called CanberraAIBoycott has sparked debate over whether small businesses and charities should be judged for using A...
canberra.content:
AI’s everywhere … is it time for consumers to fight back? Photo: Jarryd Rowley.

A new Instagram page called CanberraAIBoycott has sparked debate over whether small businesses and charities should be judged for using AI advertising.

While the argument rages online, marketing professionals have backed small businesses using AI, saying that, if used properly like any other tool, it can help them advertise cheaply and broadly.

The new page started after Audrey Taylor posted on Reddit about how tired she was of AI posters and flyers.

The reaction went semi-viral and led her to create the Instagram page, which posts screenshots of businesses, charities and events that use AI in their marketing.

“The idea for the original post came after I visited a local attraction that I go to every year to honour my Dad, who passed away seven years ago.

“I noticed that the graphic design on their flyers had been done by AI. It was really disappointing because it’s one of the most photographed places in the ACT and it had been covered with something that wasn’t real,” Ms Taylor said.

“That led me to make a post on the Canberra subreddit, which blew up. I realised that there actually was a need, and people wanted to have more of a voice about this, and so I created the Instagram page.”

Ms Taylor said the basic, easily recognisable designs used for posters and flyers create an instant disconnect for her and many others who view AI content.

“One of the core reasons I believe that businesses use AI is because it’s the easiest thing to use,” she said.

“You can generate almost anything and quickly. The problem is, they all look the same, and they flood social media feeds.

“They’re all crowded with information, they have this almost cartoon-like appearance, and it’s impossible to take seriously.

“I believe if you want to engage with the community, you have to engage with the community.

“That includes using artists or graphic designers to create things and using the creators who have actually studied advertising and marketing, and who know how to make advertising in the best way for businesses.”

While many have supported calling out AI-generated material, others, including the managing director at one x, Adam Gill, said using AI as a marketing tool makes sense as a cost-effective way for smaller organisations to advertise.

“Plenty of businesses can’t afford a designer or an agency. It’s the same with events or organisations run by volunteers who are doing their work outside of their full-time job. There isn’t always the time or means to market themselves,” Mr Gill said.

“So, if it’s the difference between them doing marketing or not doing marketing, I’m all for them using AI.

“With that said, AI should be looked at as a tool in the same way that Canva and Photoshop are.

“There’s a difference between using it to create a headline or format a poster with information and creating fake images from the ground up. I think where businesses can miss out is with their ability to use AI to stand out.”

Mr Gill said using AI requires a skill set, including writing thorough prompts, reworking outputs and adding a human element to the final product.

“Audiences are way smarter than people think, and if something feels fake, they will notice it, and they will remember it,” Mr Gill said.

“The risk with AI content is, if something looks generic or misleads people, they’ll distance themselves from it.

“Just this morning I was getting AI ads for a plumber, a pub, a flooring company and a tutoring company, and they all look the same, even though they’re different industries.

“They’re targeting different audiences, but they all look the same with that AI shine and tint to it. Businesses need to be able to identify that and rework it.

“It’s all about building their skill sets with AI. Are they using in-depth prompts that really drive home what they’re trying to sell? Are they uploading real images to be used in the marketing?

“All of these things go towards creating something with AI that does stand out.”

Mr Gill said he understands that the core argument against AI is to support creatives and support local businesses, but he believes that can still be achieved with proper use of AI.

“Our view is that businesses earn trust by being honest about how they operate,” he said.

“To boycott businesses because of that is quite extreme.

“We just need to take a minute to understand these businesses, their circumstances and how they can best use AI to express themselves creatively.

“Again, if it’s used properly, it can be a very useful marketing tool.

“If their skill sets with AI aren’t there and there’s a level of dishonesty with what they generate, that’s when businesses lose people with what they put out.”

canberra.title: Street Fighter is a train wreck … and you’re gonna love it
canberra.snippet: This year has been bookended by two video game-inspired movies based on beloved fighting games that have been around for decades. We star...
canberra.content:
Street Fighter is the second movie this year based on a long-running fighting game series, following Mortal Kombat II. Photo: Paramount Pictures.

This year has been bookended by two video game-inspired movies based on beloved fighting games that have been around for decades.

We started with Mortal Kombat II in May, a pretty lacklustre experience with a couple of fun set pieces that, at the very least, made it watchable.

Now, as we near the end of the year, Street Fighter takes its turn trying to appeal to the masses with a new big-screen outing.

But which heavyweight wins the big-budget bout?

Well … It’s a draw.

Street Fighter follows Ken (Noah Centineo) and Ryu (Andrew Koji), two young fighters adopted by the same mentor, Gouken. In 1987, Ryu is invited to the World Warrior Tournament, which pits the best fighters on Earth against each other.

Ryu wins the tournament, but shortly after his victory, Gouken is murdered by a dark entity that wishes to absorb Ryu’s abilities. Following the death of their father figure, Ryu goes into hiding while Ken drinks himself into obscurity.

Several years later, both Ken and Ryu are recruited by the mysterious Chun Li (Callina Liang) to take part in the second iteration of the World Warrior Tournament, which has been backed by the power-hungry dictator M. Bison (David Dastmalchian).

Street Fighter was never going to have a super grounded plot with expert writing and explorable themes. It was always going to be a silly story with a crazy cast of characters, loud soundtracks and vibrant visuals.

To the movie’s credit, it does do all of those things. The issue is that it doesn’t translate into a coherent narrative; instead, it feels like a parody of the very thing it’s adapting.

Minor spoilers for the film, but several scenes throughout serve as backstory or flashbacks. When these scenes take place, they are presented in anime-style animation.

This matters because these scenes perfectly capture the over-the-top nature of the games.

The flips and tricks, the ridiculous costumes and the crazy fights are all impressive, and the animation feels like it respects the grandiose nature of the source material. However, in live-action, it all looks tacky and like very expensive Halloween costumes.

Like Mortal Kombat before it, aside from the fights themselves, it comes across as a strange parody.

Nothing is properly fleshed out, character motivations are very surface-level, and aside from one or two cast members really trying, everything feels like a joke.

With something as exaggerated as Street Fighter, if the film doesn’t respect itself, how is anyone supposed to watch it?

That said, there is something strangely charming about the film. Not in an ‘I’m going to watch this on repeat’ kind of way, but more like a ‘I could put this on while I’m cleaning’ kind of way.

This is largely due to the film’s aesthetic. It is bright, it is loud, and the fights are fun. Coincidentally, you don’t have to think about any of these too much when watching a movie.

It’s very much in the vein of turning your brain off and letting the flashy things flash in front of you, and in that sense, the movie works.

The issue is, if you’re paying $25-plus to see a movie at the cinema, I’m not too sure many people will want to turn their brains off.

When it comes to using any critical thinking, Street Fighter falls apart at the seams. It doesn’t think its own plot is strong enough to fully flesh out. Many of the characters are shallow, and nothing groundbreaking reinvents the franchise.

But as a train wreck of nonsense, it is quite enjoyable to sit back and watch the tomfoolery.

It comes down to this: if you want a live-action reimagining of the games you’ve played for decades, you’ll be disappointed. If you want a silly two-hour romp that doesn’t care much about being anything, you’ll have fun.

Street Fighter is now showing in cinemas across the country.

canberra.title: 4000 km and a tandem bike: These fellas are raising money for human and canine welfare
canberra.snippet: Two dog-loving cyclists are about to embark on a challenging 4000 km journey from Perth to Canberra on a tandem bike to raise money for L...
canberra.content:
Bryce Taylor and Michael Matheson-Deng will begin their 4000 km trek on 1 November to continue supporting many of the ACT’s kennel dogs, including Tofu. Photo: Jarryd Rowley.

Two dog-loving cyclists are about to embark on a challenging 4000 km journey from Perth to Canberra on a tandem bike to raise money for Lifeline and Dogs Canberra.

Michael Matheson-Deng and Bryce Taylor will begin their charity ride, Ride for Ruff Days, in Perth on 1 November, and will aim to arrive in Canberra within 40 days.

Both Michael and Bryce are executives at Dogs Canberra, a service that trains kennel dogs while giving Canberra community members a chance to walk and interact with them.

“Dogs Canberra is a dual-purpose organisation. We support animal welfare, but we also do a lot for mental health empowerment in the community, especially through the community dog-walking program,” Michael said.

“There are huge connections between having good mental health and having a pet, but Canberra is a very transient city.

“People are always coming and going, a lot of people are students, and it’s tricky to have that long-term commitment of a pet. We think that bridging the gap between not having a pet and the accessibility of having a pet in the community is really important.

“Through Dogs Canberra, we’re able to give people the opportunity to meet and pet dogs without the responsibility of looking after them full time. By doing this ride, we are looking to raise money for our organisation so we can keep offering that opportunity.”

Yoshi and Tofu are just a couple of the lovable canine companions Dogs Canberra supports. Photo: Jarryd Rowley.

Bryce said the idea for the ride began about 18 months ago. He explained that he and Michael were both looking for something challenging to base their fundraising effort on.

“We’re just the average Joes. We’re not Ironmen, but we wanted to do something that would push ourselves,” Bryce said.

“I ride a bike fairly often, Michael not so much, but we came up with the idea of doing a tandem bike ride from Perth to Canberra. It’s about as long a ride as you can do, 4000 km, and it’s going to take us about 40 days to finish.

“We will start the trip in Perth, then head down to the town of Esperance before cutting across the Nullarbor. From there, we will travel to Adelaide along the coast, all the way through to Melbourne.

“During the final couple of hundred kilometres, which will be from Jindabyne to Canberra, a few other riders will come and join us and make a real community event of it.”

Bryce said tandem bikes bring a little extra challenge that traditional bikes don’t.

“With the tandem specifically, it takes a lot of practice to get used to,” he said.

“Changing gears, going around bends and things like that all require communication. It’s taken Michael and I a little bit to get familiar with but we’re pretty confident now.”

Both Michael and Bryce said the journey is about encouraging conversations around mental health and reminding Australians that it’s okay to struggle and ask for help.

“Ride for Ruff Days is all about letting people know that it really is ok to struggle,” Michael said.

“Bryce and I aren’t athletes by any means and we will no doubt struggle across this ride, but we will have support, and there’s support for others struggling right now too.

“Services like Lifeline, which can be called on 13 11 14, are there to support people who are struggling. The money we raise will be split 50-50 between them and the work we do at Dogs Canberra.”

To donate to Michael and Bryce’s ride or learn more about Dogs Canberra, the events they host and the work they do, visit the Dogs Canberra website here.

canberra.title: I’ve lived in Canberra my whole life, so why do I feel like a tourist?
canberra.snippet: Damn this ever-evolving city! Things are never where I left them! I’ve lived in Canberra my whole life, but lately I have no idea where I...
canberra.content:
I could have sworn I left a carpark here. Photo: Hayley Nicholls.

Damn this ever-evolving city! Things are never where I left them!

I’ve lived in Canberra my whole life, but lately I have no idea where I am. Or where to park.

For context, I’m a Canberra ’80s baby and a rare Southside/Northside half-breed. I grew up in Chisholm (2905, represent!) before defecting to live that uni sharehouse life in Belcompton. I got married and played house in Gungahlin, before settling down for a semi-rural lifestyle over the border.

I’ve always known Canberra like the back of my hand.

I’m sure other Canberra long-termers will attest to feeling that we know every nook and cranny of our city. We’ve watched bands in every community centre, attended house parties in every street, lurked around every skate park and been sick in every back alley.

Our bush capital has always held small-town vibes and a familiar, comfortable, reliable sameness.

So, a public service announcement for Canberrans who haven’t ventured into Civic lately: Prepare to be humbled. And build in a buffer.

Now a 40-year-old mother of two, living border-adjacent and often working from home, it’s not often I find myself travelling “into town”.

But recently, I was lured by the thrill of seeing Region’s own Briony Winchester appear as part of the Canberra Writers Festival.

Gathering a group of similar suburban-dwelling mamas, we planned drinks at Verity Lane, dinner at Dear Prudence before the show at Smith’s Alternative.

And if that sounded like gobbledygook to you, you’re not alone. This is a safe space.

If you – like us – are more comfortable meeting at Pancake Parlour, downing Midori Illusions at Insomnia, before somehow ending up at Phoenix – well, it may be time to start using eye cream. And allowing an extra half hour to get lost when you visit the city.

Between construction chaos, venue churn, and new haunts in unexpected places, trips into Civic now feel like a non-consensual escape room.

Once a smelly inlet we walked past en route to Mooseheads, Civic’s laneways are becoming home to hidden destinations – if you can navigate the construction maze and solve parking puzzles. Photo: City Renewal Authority.

Which is why our entire crew – OG Canberrans, every one – arrived late, harried and bewildered.

Except me.

I had a head start, having only recently ventured into the city for a performance at Canberra Theatre. On that occasion, it took several attempts before I found safe passage into the one remaining carpark I knew of, which was overflowing and bordered by barricades. By the time I sensed my way to the theatre, I’d had enough drama for one night.

Not this time, Civic! I thought.

Allowing time for detours, dead ends, parking and panic attacks, I left the house two weeks ago to arrive on time.

At 6:31 pm, a stream of ‘I’ll be late’ texts trickled in, before my dinner companions drip-fed into the laneway – all having parked in inventive locales and conveying their shock at finding Canberra looking so grown-up as to be almost unrecognisable.

Laneways? Trams? Scooters? A lack of free and easy parking?

Who turned my beloved bush capital into an actual city, and why was I not consulted?

With every new development discussion comes the question of who we’re developing Canberra for. The long-term residents? Its transient community of workers and students? Or outsiders, whom we’re desperate to convince there’s more to Canberra than Parliament and Questacon?

I suppose that’s how cities and tourism work. Not everything is designed solely with residents in mind. How rude.

I do wonder how all the upheaval affects our sense of identity. As our city shape-shifts continuously, it seems difficult to form a shared sense of anything (except frustration).

I’m all for progress. It’s natural, necessary and exciting. But it can also be disorientating, and, in this case, bloody inconvenient.

If change keeps coming at this speed, maybe being perpetually surprised (read: confused) by our own city will become inherently Canberran.

At the very least, we can share a sense of pride as we watch our city grow up.

For me, every outing feels like running into a kid you haven’t seen in a few years. You remember them learning to walk and eating sand, but suddenly they’re taller than you and growing facial hair, and you hear yourself saying ‘Oh my God! You’re so big! Who gave you permission to grow up?’ .

I’m proud of my hometown. It might be in an awkward teen phase right now – smiling through braces of construction fencing, pockmarked in garish yellow signage, and generally pissing off everyone within radius – but I know it will emerge eventually.

I hope we still recognise it.

canberra.title: Hollywood has found this Braidwood favourite and it’s time you did too
canberra.snippet: Braidwood’s Nepali restaurant and live music venue Smokey Horse has no business being so damn cool. Opening in 2018, but having served Ne...
canberra.content:
It’s hard to resist the pull of Smokey Horse at twilight. Photo: Tenele Conway.

Braidwood’s Nepali restaurant and live music venue Smokey Horse has no business being so damn cool.

Opening in 2018, but having served Nepalese food for the community in various forms for decades, the eclectic venue at the entrance to the heritage-listed main street is well on its way to becoming an icon in the region.

I don’t use ‘icon’ lightly. Longevity alone doesn’t earn a venue that status, but being distinct among peers does. Smokey Horse is so wonderfully weird, and so unapologetically itself, it’s already an icon in the eyes of many.

If you haven’t discovered it yet, you’re a little behind.

A recent appearance by Hollywood celebrities Jack Quaid (son of Meg Ryan and Dennis Quaid) and his Australian bride, actress Claudia Doumit, on the eve of their Mona Farm wedding has put Smoky Horse on the global map, but just as the old cliché says, it’s never too late to see what the fuss is all about (or is that two clichés?)

Smokey Horse is eclectically cool in all the right ways. Photo: Tenele Conway.

When making plans for Smokey Horse, keep a few things in mind. They can, and do, operate in opposition to their posted Google hours. If you’re making the trip from Canberra, I’d recommend booking a table on their website or calling ahead to make sure they’ll be open as expected.

Next, decide what kind of Smokey Horse experience you’re up for.

If you want a chill Friday night curry, a cold local brew and an hour or two immersed in local Braidwood life, check Facebook beforehand to make sure the night isn’t reserved for a gig.

On the other hand, if you’re drawn to an eclectic, well-curated music scene, where Ethiopian jazz one night makes way for indie alternative pop the next, check their online gig guide and plan your visit accordingly.

If you take the chill Friday-night route, as I tend to, you won’t find yourself bored in the quirky dining room.

On one side you’ll find a collection of Pop Mart toys making their home in a pot of succulents. On the other side is a superhero, one I don’t know by name, trapped in the metal rungs of a light fitting. He’s not alone: a nearby praying mantis climbs over a real bone, tiny cats peer over a seashell, and a ceramic Rick, of Rick and Morty fame, seems right at home among a collection of Buddhas. I did warn you, it’s eclectic.

The momos are a must; I like mine steamed and stuffed with pork. Photo: Martin Conway.

Chefs have come and gone over the years, but the menu has stayed true to a formula that works, delivering the punchy flavours Smokey Horse has built its reputation on.

Starting with momos (Nepalese dumplings) is a must. Choose steamed or fried and filled with pork, chicken or a vegan mixture. They’re served with house-made tomato and sesame achar (chutney). Like Romeo and Juliet, the dumplings and sauce share an unbreakable bond you should respect as you eat the tender parcels.

The menu then moves through a range of curries served on traditional thalis (metal platters designed to separate the dish’s components).

The pulled pork choila is a steal at $19. Photo: Martin Conway.

I highly recommend the pulled pork choila. Twice-cooked and rich with spices, it draws on the Kathmandu Valley’s Newari ceremonial feasting traditions.

Listed under ‘small stuff’ at $19, it rivals a main at most Canberra restaurants, and the generous portion shows the value on offer here.

The sides here are just as important as the meat, with the carrot salad adding a sweet crunch and the tart daikon achar cutting through the richness. A pappadum is thrown in for good measure, and the chiura (beaten rice) brings a rare cultural element to the fore.

For a larger Thali-style meal, the Nepali chicken curry thali with rice, lentil dahl, seasonal vegetables and greens in garlic butter is a crowd pleaser.

The curry thalis are generous and delicious. Photo: Martin Conway.

For vegetarians, there is a veg curry thali and Kwati: a spiced red bean and potato stew served with paratha, a dish also connected to Newari traditions.

KFC happens to make an appearance, not the kind you might expect, but Smokey Horse’s own version, which they jokingly call Kathmandu Fried Chicken. They also have crispy chicken wings if you want to double down on the crunchy chicken.

If I haven’t yet enticed you with the promise of damn good curry to be eaten in an eclectic space where you may spot a celebrity, there is also an extensive menu of spirits, local beers and local wines, including a nice selection of wines from the nearby producers Sapling Yard in Bungendore and Long Rail Gully in Murrumbateman.

If you’re tempted to linger over a glass or two, especially by the firepit, consider it time well spent. Coolness can be absorbed by osmosis, so drag your feet, and you might just leave a whole new you.

Smokey Horse is located at 183 Wallace Street, Braidwood. They’re open Thursday to Sunday from 3 pm until late.

australia.title: A place in the history books but no toastie: my time on board Western Sydney airport’s inaugural flight
australia.snippet: The mood is jubilant on the Airbus A320 Neo as aviation enthusiasts and locals thrill at their place on the first flight Western Sydney a...
australia.content:
My journey begins at 3.57am when I step out on to the street in Enmore, wheeling a small suitcase.

I’m going to catch the inaugural flight from the new Western Sydney international airport on Sunday morning, operated by Jetstar. The enormous $5.3bn greenfield development more than 40 years in the making is opening its architecturally lauded halls to commercial passengers, with significant fanfare.

There will be 188 passengers onboard JQ362, with 30 seats reserved for media and VIP guests and the other 158 sold out in just 45 minutes, according to the airline. I get to be a part of this history-making moment. But first, I have to get there.

While the flight’s not until 11am, media have been asked to get to the airport about 7am, which means I need to leave at a very early hour if I’m going to test out the transport links from where I’m staying in Sydney’s inner west. A dedicated airport shuttle from Central station won’t leave early enough.

Resisting the temptation to catch an Uber and following Google Maps’ best suggested route, I walk to Stanmore and catch the N50 bus to Liverpool, where I wait for about 15 minutes to get on the 860 bus to WSI, one of several new local routes servicing the airport.

We travel along a main road past sprawling strip malls that give way to large semi-rural properties and eventually paddocks. The sun rises.

By the time I arrive at the airport at 6.35am, I’ve spent more time on buses than I will on the plane. Of course, it will likely be more convenient for those coming from somewhere in western Sydney, the Blue Mountains or even Canberra.

It takes ages but it’s all pretty seamless. As we step off the bus, I get chatting to John Ung, a Cabramatta local who was keen to check out the airport. “This was like, nothing,” he says, gesturing over the 1,800-hectare block in front of us, which was once farmland but now houses two sparkling new terminals, a landscaped garden and a car park.

“It’s about time that Sydney has a second international airport,” Ung says. His first impressions? “It’s nice, but not finished yet”. A metro station, for example, has been delayed until at least December 2027.

Walking into the airport feels like getting into a brand new car. It smells a bit like one too. Three architecture firms delivered the “once-in-a-generation infrastructure project”, whose walls are lined with panels hewn from local sandstone. I definitely could have got here later, I think as I browse the kiosk, where packaged sandwiches will set you back a cool $11.95. A couple of food outlets are still to open but, apart from that, everything seems pretty ready to go.

Following Jetstar, six airlines have committed to WSI, with Air New Zealand to operate the first international flight on Monday. The New South Wales government is subsidising most of the international airlines and the airport’s success depends on their ongoing commitment. The Jetstar chief executive, Steph Tully, seems confident about WSI. She says fares will generally be cheaper than at Kingsford Smith, they have already added additional services to the Gold Coast and are eyeing flights to Bali.

Chris Grant, a longtime St Marys resident I meet at the bag drop, is flying to the Gold Coast and back on Sunday, to Auckland on Monday, and to Europe via Singapore Airlines on its first flight from WSI in November. “I really wanted to be on the first flights so, as soon as they were announced, I booked,” Grant says. “The western suburbs have grown up – now they’re an international destination.”

There’s lots of excitement. Staff are handing out Jetstar merchandise and a person dressed as the airline’s cartoon plane mascot is wandering around. Most passengers that I speak to are travel enthusiasts or western Sydney locals. “I’m just excited,” says James Irwin from Penrith, who is wearing an orange Jetstar hat. “To be a part of history … it’s beyond words”.

The official opening event is held in the international terminal. Its guests include many politicians past and present, as well as the family of Nancy Bird-Walton, the pioneering aviator for whom the airport is named.

Addressing the crowd, the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, says it’s an “extraordinary day”. As he’s talking, punters are gathering in the adjoining domestic terminal to watch the first flight take off, many of them in orange hats and taking photos at the windows. I’ve got to go board the plane.

The mood is jubilant on the Airbus A320 Neo. There are many rounds of cheers and applause, including for the cabin crew and pilots. The first officer, Aglaya Papadokokolakis, is a 25-year-old from Blacktown who said the flight was a “pinch me moment” and whose mum surprised her onboard.

I’m seated next to Alexander Lau and Daniel Kirkwood from Wolli Creek, who say Jetstar flights are usually cheaper from WSI than Kingsford Smith, at least at the moment. Their first impressions are that international flights are more expensive at WSI but they hope this will change as more services come online.

While there was sparkling wine and hors d’oeuvres on offer at the opening event, and an optional Jetstar cookie for passengers at the boarding gate, there’s no catering on board. The flight is so quick the crew run out of time to finish the service down the back of the plane, where I’m seated. I’d contemplated getting a $15 ham and cheese toastie for the full Jetstar experience.

australia.title: ‘Unusually large’ multi-state storm causing severe weather for Australia’s east – with more on the way
australia.snippet: BoM predicts hail, damaging winds, flash flooding and power outages across southern Queensland, western NSW, the ACT and eastern Victoria...
australia.content:
Large parts of eastern Australia were put on alert for severe thunderstorms on Sunday afternoon with more potential storms and flood risk in store for Monday.

On Sunday afternoon, the Bureau of Meteorology issued a severe thunderstorm warning for Sydney, greater Wollongong and parts of Blue Mountains, Hawkesbury, Gosford, Wyong and Wollondilly, Wingecarribee areas.

BoM said a broad line of storms had already swept through western New South Wales, while eight flood warnings were in place across southern Queensland after days of torrential rain.

Severe thunderstorms that could bring hail, damaging winds, flash flooding and power outages were likely over a huge area on Sunday afternoon, the bureau said, including across southern Queensland, western NSW, the ACT and eastern Victoria.

Wind gusts of up to 100km/h were recorded in the central west of NSW around midday on Sunday.

“This is a multi-state system of storms and it’s unusually large,” said bureau meteorologist David Crock.

Crock said an area of high pressure had been sitting over the Tasman Sea for the past 10 days that had been blocking weather fronts and bringing storms and rains to southern Queensland.

“Eventually you get a strong enough system that pushes that blocking pattern away and that typically brings severe weather with it,” he said.

A front of cooler air was moving from the west on Sunday afternoon, dragging in tropical moisture from the north and bringing storm conditions to central parts of NSW and to Canberra on Sunday afternoon.

“We have a big line of storms that’s extending all the way from the Snowy mountains to the Queensland border. Behind that we are watching to see if there’s going to another band developing behind it.”

Storm activity was likely to continue through Sunday evening and into Monday in northern NSW and southern Queensland as the cold front continued to push.

“[Monday] is the last big bang of this system and that’s going to be a great relief for those people in south-east Queensland,” he said.

Southern parts of Queensland had been through a weather “whiplash” in the past week, Crock said.

Some eight flood warnings were in place over southern Queensland. The Mary River downstream of Gympie was forecast to reach major flood levels in Tiaro on Sunday evening and into Monday.

After a very dry September, southern parts of the state had seen October rainfall “multiple times their average” for the month, Crock said, with areas around the Sunshine Coast seeing between 200mm and 400mm of rain in the past week.

In the south-east, coastal showers are expected across Victoria and Tasmania, with snow falling above 800m above sea level in Tasmania.

In Western Australia, cooler weather continues on Monday, with showers possible in parts of the south west.

The bureau’s current long-range forecast for November to January suggests rainfall is likely to be above average over most of the country except the far north and much of Tasmania.

November is likely to be warmer than usual for the southern half of the continent, with night-time temperatures in particular forecast to be likely well above average over most of the country.

Global heating has seen Australia warm by about 1.5C since 1910, the bureau’s long-term climate data shows.

australia.title: AFP boss says politicians’ heated rhetoric is fuelling threats against MPs
australia.snippet: Commissioner Krissy Barrett says women are more often singled out, often with threats of sexual violence Get our breaking news email , fr...
australia.content:
Australia’s top federal law enforcement official has drawn a direct link between politicians’ rhetoric and threats and abuse being directed at leaders.

The safety of elected representatives at all levels has been thrown into the spotlight after independent MP Helen Haines was allegedly deliberate attacked outside her Wangaratta electoral office.

Haines remains in a serious but stable condition at the Alfred hospital in Melbourne, following her double leg amputation.

The Australian federal police commissioner, Krissy Barrett, said there was no doubt the threat environment had changed for politicians.

“When I start work every morning, one of the first things I do is read a report … [that] summarises all of the threats that have been reported to the AFP over the last 24 hours,” she told the ABC’s Insiders program.

“Now, some days that report is pages and pages long.”

The commissioner said she wasn’t interested in policing free speech or intervening in political discourse.

“But I would challenge any Australian to read some of these threats and some of the abuse that is reported to us from federal parliamentarians and for anyone to argue that that is free speech or political discourse,” she added.

The move from the sending of physical hate mail to online threats had played a significant role in the increasing volume of worrying material, while also highlighting the influence of inflammatory political imagery and language.

“We do see where there is particular political conflict or discourse occurring … it does have a direct correlation to what we see in terms of threats and abuse, and sometimes it’s very immediate,” Barrett said.

Past One Nation cartoons depicting political figures, including the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, being hit by cars or buses have resurfaced in the days since the alleged attack on Haines.

The AFP commissioner said there was “a reaction amongst the community” to material such as the cartoons.

The policing agency, which is responsible for protecting federal politicians and office-holders, has held a number of emergency safety briefings with parliamentarians since Monday.

Male and female MPs were targeted equally with threats and abuse, Barrett said, but women were more often singled out individually, often with threats of sexual violence.

“My hope is that this really causes people to pause and have a think about what’s happening in this country and the impact of that,” she said.

“And if this is not the incident, then what is?”

Federal MPs from across the political spectrum have acknowledged the difficulty in balancing their personal security and access to voters.

“As a local MP, I don’t want to stop going to community events,” Liberal frontbencher Ted O’Brien told News24 on Sunday.

“That open access is a cornerstone of democracy. We’re particularly good at it in Australia. We can’t take away grassroots politics.”

Labor minister Catherine King said she has been contending with the deteriorating safety for some time.

“It is when, not if, that something will happen to one of us and we’ve been saying that certainly for the last five years or so,” she said.

“I had a mobile caravan for almost 25 years. I don’t use that now because it doesn’t have a second exit point.

“If someone did kick off and I’m trapped in the van, it’s very hard to deal with that.”

australia.title: ‘Horrific’: woman, 19, shot in head in drive-by shooting outside boxing event near Brisbane
australia.snippet: Offenders still at large after shots fired from vehicle outside licensed premises in Loganholme Get our breaking news email , free app or...
australia.content:
Four people have been injured after a drive-by shooting outside a venue hosting a boxing event, including a 19-year-old woman who was shot in the head.

Queensland police Detective Inspector Ian Galpin said a group of people were gathered at the passenger drop-off zone outside Fitzy’s Loganholme, south of Brisbane, about 8.18pm on Saturday when a Mitsubishi pulled up.

Galpin said police would allege a “number of shots” were fired from the front window of the pub where two males wearing balaclavas and gloves were sitting, striking four people.

A Jimboomba woman, 19, was shot in the neck and head. She has undergone surgery and remains in a critical condition.

Speaking on Sunday, Galpin described her as an “innocent bystander”.

“It’s horrific. It’s something that her family should never have to go through.”

Three others were injured and remained in serious but stable conditions: a Browns Plains man, 38, shot in the abdomen and arm, a Salisbury man, 37, shot in the abdomen, and a Cornubia man, 27, shot in the abdomen.

Galpin alleged the Mitsubishi was set alight on Maloney Road at Waterford West, which was declared a crime scene, while a second car collected the occupants of the Mitsubishi and departed.

“It is possible one of these persons from the Mitsubishi was injured or burnt during this process,” Galpin said.

Galpin said it was too soon to say whether it was related to organised crime.

“This is a horrific event in a public space where adults and children were simply trying to enjoy a sporting event and this incident, it’s clearly not acceptable. We will not tolerate it.”

Speaking on Sunday morning, Logan’s mayor, Jon Raven, described residents in the area as frightened.

“This has sent a shock wave through Logan. We’ve never seen something like this in Logan before,” Raven told the Today show.

“Our hearts go out obviously to the victims and the staff and the people at this boxing event.

“I’ve been to one of these events before, they’re [a] really family friendly environment, and I know there’s lots of children who were there, and this will impact them for the rest of their lives.”

The deputy commander of Queensland police, Chris Stream, described the scene as “confronting”.

“A number of people had suffered gunshot wounds,” he told Today.

Raven said the event had been organised to help children steer clear of violence.

“[The organiser] will be devastated this has happened because he loves boxing and uses it as a tool to empower and reconnect young people who might be going off the rails, and this is the opposite of what he’ll want to see,” Raven said.

Logan City Titles shared a statement on social media on Sunday morning.

“We are heartbroken about the incident that occurred at the fight night,” it read.

“Logan City Titles was a family event, an event for our community, showcasing local talent, hard work and everyone’s skills inside the ring.

“These types of incidents have no place in the boxing community or any part of the broader community.”

The offenders were still at large on Sunday but police said they did not believe there was an ongoing threat to the public.

Police were urging anyone with information to contact them.

australia.title: DanceRites 2026: First Nations performers bring story, song and dance to Sydney Opera House – in pictures
australia.snippet: More 300 First Nations dancers gathered at the Sydney Opera House forecourt over the weekend to compete in the DanceRites festival, a nat...
australia.content:
More 300 First Nations dancers gathered at the Sydney Opera House forecourt over the weekend to compete in the DanceRites festival, a national competition celebrating Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander culture. Now in its ninth year, DanceRites invites everyone to join in the living history of Tubowgule (the Dharug word for Bennelong Point), a place where story, song and dance has long been shared. This year’s event honoured the legacy of Aunty Rhoda Roberts, who died in March and was formerly the head of First Nations programming at the Sydney Opera House

DanceRites 2026 is free and runs until Sunday 25 October at the Sydney Opera House

world.title: Mystery over source of Ebola infection in Nigeria fuels concern about spread of virus
world.snippet: Switzerland says patient is wife of Swiss diplomat and believed to have contracted virus while travelling in Uganda Health officials acro...
world.content:
Health officials across Africa are racing to determine how Nigeria’s first Ebola patient ⁠in more than a decade ⁠became infected, amid fears ​the outbreak could spread further after reaching a fourth African country.

The Swiss foreign ministry said on Friday the patient in Nigeria, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja, had not travelled to the Democratic Republic of ⁠Congo, where the outbreak was first detected in mid-May before spreading to Uganda, Kenya and now Nigeria. The woman was believed to have contracted Ebola while travelling with her husband in Uganda, the ministry added.

The new information contradicts accounts from Uganda, which previously said the woman had travelled to eastern DR Congo, and will raise concerns about the ability of authorities to contain the outbreak, which is already the most geographically widespread in history.

The Ugandan government reported Ebola cases in May and June before WHO declared it Ebola-free in August. A Ugandan government spokesperson told Reuters on Thursday that Uganda had no ​Ebola cases and that, if ​it did, it would make that information ​public.

The World Health Organization said investigations were continuing to establish the likely source of infection for the Ebola patient in Nigeria.

The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention is investigating whether the patient may have come into contact with an Ebola patient in Kenya, as both travelled from Uganda’s Entebbe airport on 3 October, said Dr Wessam Mankoula, head of emergency preparedness and response at the organisation.

Catherine Smallwood, a WHO Ebola incident manager in DR Congo, told a UN briefing in Geneva via video ‌link on Friday that WHO staff in DR Congo had no information showing the patient in Nigeria had travelled to the country.

Smallwood said a link to the case in Kenya was possible, ​but added that officials would need to compare the timing with when the Nigeria patient’s symptoms began to tell whether the infection more likely happened at the Ugandan airport or elsewhere.

Marion Koopmans, a Dutch virologist and member of the WHO’s Ebola emergency committee, cast doubt on the theory. “I think that is very speculative unless there is evidence of sharing the same ​space in a manner that could explain that,” she said. “Random presence at the same location, a large airport, is not a supported epidemiological link by any standard of what we currently know.”

The Nigerian health minister, Muhammad Ali Pate, said Nigeria’s case remains contained and that contact-tracing was continuing. “We are trying to contain it so it doesn’t go out to the communities. Hopefully, it won’t get to that and we are working hard to ensure that,” Pate said.

Melaku Yirga, vice-president for Africa at Prosper Global (formerly Mercy Corps), said the confirmation of Ebola in Kenya and Nigeria reinforces the need for countries to work closely together to prevent further transmission.

“What matters most now is speed, sharing information across borders without delay and ensuring frontline health workers and local organiaations have the resources to respond quickly,” he said.

Ebola is a highly contagious and often fatal viral disease that affects humans and non-human primates. It spreads through body fluids or contaminated materials and causes organ damage, blood vessel impairment and sometimes severe internal and external bleeding.

The current outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no approved treatment or vaccine. It was first announced on 15 May and has infected more than 9,500 people and killed nearly half of them.

The outbreak is the largest and deadliest in DR Congo’s history and second only ​globally to ​the 2014-16 outbreak in west Africa, which infected ​more than ‌28,600 people ​and ​killed more than 11,000.

Reuters and the Associated Press contributed reporting

world.title: Lewis Hamilton aims to extend career till early 2030s so he can race in African Grand Prix
world.snippet: 41-year-old set on ‘dream to be able to race in Africa’ Rwanda to host despite criticism of human rights record Lewis Hamilton has said h...
world.content:
Lewis Hamilton has said he hopes to remain racing in Formula One until he can take part in the African Grand Prix which is set to take place in Rwanda in the 2030s. The seven-time world champion believes it is right that F1 is to hold a race there despite criticism of the country’s human rights record.

Last week F1 confirmed Rwanda was to host the African Grand Prix having concluded a 10-year agreement for the meeting on a purpose-built circuit, with the first race set for the early 2030s. It is lined up to be held on a circuit in Bugesera, 25 miles south of the capital, Kigali, which has yet to be constructed and marks a return to the African continent for the first time since it last held a race at Kyalami, South Africa in 1993.

Hamilton has been championing a race in Africa for some time. The 41-year-old is understood to be currently contracted with Ferrari until the end of the 2027 season, and speaking before this weekend’s US Grand Prix he said he would like to continue racing for at least another four years in order to make it to the meeting in Rwanda.

“I’m now forced to have to stay a lot longer because we have a race in Africa and that’s been my dream to be able to race in Africa,” he said. “So, I have to keep fighting to try and stay fit if I can. If I can still punch out good results over the next year, we’ll keep it going.”

Hamilton would be at least in his mid-40s if he was to continue until 2030. F1’s current oldest driver is 45-year-old Fernando Alonso.

F1’s deal with Rwanda is for a 10-year period but because of the country’s human rights record the award of the race has been criticised as an act of sportswashing.

“A 10-year grand prix ‘presented by Visit Rwanda’ is a sportswashing prize for the Rwandan authorities,” said Felix Jakens, Amnesty UK’s head of campaigns. “Rwanda is buying into the world’s biggest sports to polish its image and deflect from ⁠its appalling human rights record. Formula One says sport can be ‘a positive force for good’. That rings hollow if F1 shrugs off who it is partnering with. Rwanda’s authorities are prolific in arbitrary detention, torture and the repression of free speech.”

Hamilton nonetheless felt the meeting would serve as a force for good in Africa and that there also should be more education about the continent.

“I’m really, really hopeful for that grand prix,” he said. “Of course, I don’t get to choose where we go, and naturally there’s problems all over the world today, so I’ve seen many of the stories but I think we really have to approach it with humility.

“There’s a lot that we don’t know. I mean, growing up in England, they never ever taught us anything about Africa. It needs to be on the curriculum. A lot of the problems they have there are still results of colonialism, and the West intervening.

“I really hope, and I still have hopes, that Africa unites. I know there’s many people that don’t want that to happen, because they would be so powerful if they did, but I’m still hopeful that at some stage they will.”

The new race is being backed by the government of Rwanda and the Rwanda Development Board, who intend to develop the venue as a destination not only for motorsport but for promoting economic growth. The country has recently invested heavily in hosting sporting events, including cycling’s road world championships, cricket’s Women’s Challenge Trophy, the 2023 Fifa congress and the Basketball Africa League.

Hamilton felt that at least the race would present an opportunity for people to take a greater interest in Africa.

“Going doesn’t mean that you neglect the things that are happening there,” he said. “Hopefully many people start to educate themselves a little bit more of what is happening there, what has happened there for hundreds of years and I hope that does spark the conversation. Then I guess I’ll finish it off with, I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine. I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping that at some stage we get to.”

Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli goes into this weekend’s US Grand Prix in a position to clinch his first F1 title. The 20-year-old holds a 102-point lead over his teammate George Russell and will become Formula One’s youngest world champion if he wins, Russell finishes ninth or lower and Hamilton is fifth or lower.

world.title: Controversial US-backed vaccine trial in African newborns halted
world.snippet: Hepatitis B study in Guinea-Bissau that was to be funded by CDC and that drew global backlash ‘will not move forward’ The US-backed hepat...
world.content:
The US-backed hepatitis B vaccine trial in African newborns that drew global backlash was halted, the lead researcher said on Wednesday.

It was “now clear” that the study “will not move forward in Guinea-Bissau”, Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer, a Danish researcher, wrote on LinkedIn, adding, “we were not given the necessary governmental approval.”

The minister of health in Guinea-Bissau, Quinhin Nantote, previously denied that the project would move forward. “This is not even remotely true,” Nantote told the Guardian in Portuguese last week.

The study was to be funded with $1.6m from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), along with another $1.6m from private partners like the Bill Ackman-backed Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation.

“The solution is clear here: take the money and vaccinate as many kids as you can,” said Paul Offit, a vaccines expert at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, who sharply criticized the proposed study as unethical.

The government of Guinea-Bissau now has control over the researchers’ vaccines, which they apprehended when they searched the offices of the Bandim Health Project on Monday.

It was vital to support Guinea-Bissau in rolling the immunizations out to all newborns as soon as possible, Offit said. Guinea-Bissau currently plans to offer the universal birth dose in 2028.

The Danish researchers, led by Schaltz-Buchholzer, Christine Stabell Benn and Peter Aaby, hypothesized giving live vaccines, like the Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG), may have an overall mortality benefit beyond simply preventing illnesses like tuberculosis – but giving another vaccine like hepatitis B alongside it could dampen that effect.

Such a hypothesis was “fanciful” because the hepatitis B vaccine is a single protein among billions encountered by the immune system each day, Offit said.

“There’s no evidence for that, and it doesn’t make biological sense,” he continued. He also added that there was a very clear benefit to giving the vaccine to babies as soon as possible, because of high rates of hepatitis B in the country and the possibility of lifelong illness and death from infection.

The Danish researchers did not respond by press time to questions about the study or to this criticism. The CDC did not respond by press time to questions about whether the funding, which was appropriated through its global health work, would now be used to roll out the vaccine to all newborns in Guinea-Bissau, as recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO).

“WHO recommends that all infants receive a first dose of the hepatitis B vaccine as soon as possible after birth – preferably within 24 hours – followed by at least two additional doses,” said Tarik Jašarević, a WHO spokesperson. “WHO remains committed to working with national authorities, researchers, and partners to ensure that all newborns – in Guinea‑Bissau and worldwide – receive timely, evidence‑based protection against hepatitis B.”

Those who declined participation in the study would not have received the vaccines – making true informed consent impossible, experts say.

“Imagine you’re a mother. You want to do the best for your child,” said Henrik Støvring, a Danish researcher who has co-published research raising questions about previous research from the Bandim project.

“If they decide to participate in the trial, they have a 50% chance of getting the vaccine for their children. But if they stay out, they have a 0% chance of getting the vaccine. So how can you say that’s a non-coercive informed consent?” Støvring asked.

The proposed trial led to distrust among Bissau-Guineans, who wondered if the vaccine – which has a decades-long record of being safe and effective – was being tested on Africans because it was dangerous, Schaltz-Buchholzer said in his post.

It “should be clear” that both birth vaccination schedules – with or without hepatitis B – are not “dangerous to anyone”, he wrote. There is a clear benefit to giving hepatitis B vaccines at birth, and not doing so can lead to lifelong danger, experts say.

Conducting a study like this “makes the case that there’s something that’s worthy of study, for which they have no evidence”, Offit said.

“We have millions and millions, arguably hundreds of millions, of children in this world who have gotten that vaccine as a birth dose or haven’t. If there was any evidence that this was problematic, you would know this by now,” Offit added. “We eliminated hepatitis B in the United States in children virtually within years of starting that program, so the benefits are clear.”

Schaltz-Buchholzer also cast doubt on the effectiveness and safety of the hepatitis B vaccine at birth, noting that he believes the study was canceled because it challenges “prevailing medical assumptions, such as that HBV0 does not have non-specific effects”. The study, in addition to looking at mortality, would have also examined side-effects such as skin conditions and neurodevelopmental conditions. Dozens of studies have shown no link between vaccination and autism.

“All newborns should be given a birth dose of hepatitis B vaccine,” Offit said. “Guinea-Bissau is a country that suffers a high incidence of chronic hepatitis B. That country, more than any other country, arguably, needs to launch this program.”

world.title: Severely ill ICE detainees face imminent deportation to unknown African states, advocates say
world.snippet: Flights to third countries where the detainees have no ties are scheduled as early as Wednesday, relatives detail Send us your questions ...
world.content:
Relatives of gravely ill detainees at two Florida immigration jails say authorities are about to deport their loved ones to unknown countries in Africa despite worsening medical conditions.

Flights are scheduled as early as Wednesday, according to the families and the immigration advocacy group the Workers Circle, which has been monitoring conditions and speaking with detainees inside two Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facilities in south Florida.

The group said multiple sick detainees with varying conditions had been targeted for imminent deportation, and learned about the operation only in the last few days.

“I received a call from several detainees letting me know that men were being pulled in to interviews with deportation agents, where they were being informed that because of their medical conditions, Mexico would not be accepting their entry, and they will be sent to Africa,” Arianne Betancourt, the group’s immigrant rights organizer, said at a Tuesday-night press conference.

“We know that once they are deported and sent to these third countries, they are not receiving medical care in detention. They have difficulties getting medicine.”

A Department of Homeland Security (DHS) spokesperson, in a statement to the Guardian late on Wednesday, said it was “a false story designed to smear the brave men and women of ICE as they are facing a more than 1,600% increase in assaults against them”.

“No sick detainees are being deported. All detainees are medically cleared before travel and leave with any necessary medications.”

The affected detainees are at the Krome North processing center in Miami, which was found to be experiencing severe overcrowding by a government inspector’s report last month, and the Broward transitional center in Pompano Beach. Both facilities are privately run on behalf of ICE.

Anisley Cortés, the wife of Noslén Sendra, a 41-year-old Cuban national, said her husband had been incarcerated since last November, first at the now closed “Alligator Alcatraz” immigration jail, and at Krome since April. She said her husband has uncontrolled diabetes and acute pancreatitis that resulted in a weeks-long hospital stay earlier this year.

“He lost over 50 pounds. They wouldn’t give him his medication, and they would not give him enough food. It was a nightmare of a time for all of us,” she said. “He is very sick and needs the right healthcare.

“Cuba will not accept him as a deportee, and we now have proof that Mexico will not accept him as a deportee because he is so sick. And so they told him that because he could not be accepted at either of those two countries, ‘Oh well, we’re going to have to send you to Africa.’

“They told him that Mexico would not accept him because he has too many medications that he requires, and so they said, ‘Well, we have to deport you anyway.’ We’re left with the uncertainty of not knowing how he is, or if we’ll see him again.”

Shalyn Fluharty, an immigration rights attorney, said information from the detainees indicated deportation flights were imminent.

“We understand that just this week, within a couple of days, likely Thursday and Friday, there will be two flights going to Africa, in particular to the Central African Republic, and we also believe Burundi,” she said.

Fluharty said previously deported immigrants were shackled at their hands, ankles and waists during lengthy flights, and some who complained were placed in full body wraps with no ability to move.

“This is what we anticipate will be happening this week for these individuals, based upon what we’ve seen in the past,” she said.

“Travel can last sometimes up to 24 hours. What if you’re somebody who has a heart condition? Who has a high risk of stroke? Who is experiencing diabetes and requires regular access to food or insulin? These conditions take your already vulnerable medical state and make them, unfortunately, often life-threatening.”

The DHS statement said Sendra was “a criminal illegal alien from Cuba convicted of fraud, larceny, and property crimes” and “has been consistently cleared and discharged from the hospital following medical evaluation”.

He was ordered removed from the US in September 2015, it said.

“Third country removals are an essential public safety tool that remove the most dangerous criminal illegal aliens from our streets,” the spokesperson said.

“Illegal aliens being sent to a third country receive notice and assurances prior to their removal, and the Department of State is given diplomatic assurances from destination countries that the illegal aliens being removed there will be safe.”

Betancourt said families risked retaliation for their relatives by coming forward. “This is not a single one-off story,” she said.

“The inspector general’s report confirmed that there is a lack of medical care inside of Krome detention facility. Families have been demanding oversight, and every day they are experiencing real fear to speak up and advocate for their loved ones.”

During two unannounced visits to Krome in May, government inspectors found multiple violations of noncompliance with detention standards, including severe overcrowding. Holding 1,102 detainees in a facility with a maximum capacity of 882, the report said, “jeopardizes the safe and orderly operations within the facility”.

Other listed violations included an inadequate number of operational toilets, sinks and showers, and previous complaints included female detainees made to use toilets in full view of men, and arriving detainees held for more than 24 hours in a bus in the parking lot because of a lack of space.

Advocates say Donald Trump’s sweeping second-term immigration crackdown has caused overcrowding in detention centers nationwide that the DHS has attempted to alleviate by ramping up deportation flights to so-called third countries.

The controversial practice, approved by the US supreme court last month, has seen hundreds of detainees deported to at least a dozen African countries where they have no ties.

A Human Rights Watch report earlier this month found countless examples of abusive treatment during and after the flights, and detainees subjected to persecution, arbitrary incarceration and torture following their arrival.

world.title: Nigeria confirms Ebola case as outbreak spreads into western Africa
world.snippet: Case in Africa’s most populous country was detected in a woman who had travelled from Uganda Nigeria has confirmed an Ebola case in its c...
world.content:
Nigeria has confirmed an Ebola case in its capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus, the health ministry said.

The woman began showing symptoms on 7 October and was admitted to a hospital in Abuja four days later, where she was later diagnosed with Ebola. It is unclear when she arrived in Nigeria, Africa’s most populous country.

The health minister, Muhammad Pate, said authorities had begun tracing 44 people identified as contacts of the patient. “We are doing everything possible to contain this case by tracing all the contacts the individual may have had,” he said.

Uganda’s ministry of health said the patient had only transited through Uganda and that she is a Nigerian woman who had been on a business trip to Congo’s eastern region. The Nigerian authorities have not disclosed her nationality.

“Travel through Uganda does not establish that infection occurred here. The location of exposure remains under investigation,” the ministry said in a statement. The ministry insisted Uganda has “no confirmed active Ebola cases”.

Nigeria is the latest country to report an Ebola case as the outbreak spreads across the region. Kenya confirmed its first case earlier this month and has since recorded nine infections. Uganda had previously reported Ebola cases, but it later declared itself free of the virus.

Dr Jean Kaseya, the director general of the Africa Centers for Disease Control, said on X that “we are facing an extremely serious threat,” with a fatality rate of nearly 50% of cases.

“This Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak has already become the most geographically extensive in history, affecting several countries spread across three regions of Africa,” he said.

The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control said two weeks ago it was stepping up surveillance following the detection of Ebola in Kenya and strengthening the country’s preparedness for a potential outbreak.

“These efforts have focused on early detection, isolation and referral, laboratory diagnosis, infection prevention and control, contact tracing, risk communication and protection of health care workers,” the agency said.

Nigeria established an Ebola taskforce in June after the outbreak in Congo in mid-May.

The spread of Ebola beyond Congo has heightened fears among health authorities about the rapid transmission of the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has infected more than 9,500 people and killed more than 4,600 people.

The latest Ebola outbreak is the fastest-spreading on record and is on track to exceed the deadliest on record, the 11,000 people killed in West Africa’s regional outbreak between 2014 and 2016, WHO has said.
